# SCSS to Markdown documentation

Write exactly one Markdown page in English from the Termeh SCSS source
and documentation request supplied by the user. The page is for Termeh
developers: explain what its public APIs do and how to use them, not how
they are implemented. Always call the project "Termeh" and use the
`termeh.` namespace in examples. Never mention source file names.

The source doc comments are the primary documentation source. Read every
`///` comment, including tags, and inspect the implementation to confirm
behavior, defaults, errors, and examples. Do not invent details. If an
essential detail cannot be established, write `TODO:` at that point.

This skill only reads the supplied source files and writes the requested
Markdown page. Do not execute any commands or scripts, including shell
or terminal commands, `npm`, `git`, build, test, or version-control
commands. Do not install dependencies, run tools, or perform unrelated
repository inspection or actions. If the user does not name a folder,
produce the Markdown in chat; otherwise, save only the requested page.

## Termeh concepts

Use these concepts to understand the source. Include only the ones
relevant to the page; do not copy this section into generated pages.

- Termeh is a modern, responsive, modular CSS framework written in Sass.
  It provides ready-to-use components, responsive styling, theming,
  palettes, modifier generators, utilities, and mixins without external
  dependencies.
- A typical project configures shared values, includes the needed
  component modules, then calls `variables()` to emit the CSS custom
  properties those modules use.
- Shared configuration includes variables, palettes, gaps, and sizes.
  Define values for the default scheme and override only what changes in
  a named scheme.
- A scheme is a named theme, such as `"dark"`. Components read registered
  values as CSS variables, so switching schemes updates their appearance
  without recompiling the Sass.
- The `"base"` palette provides a scheme's main color and determines
  whether it is light or dark. Palette variants can be defined directly
  or generated by resolvers.
- Resolvers create palette variants on demand. They can be registered
  for general use or for a specific component; the two scopes are
  separate.
- Components are registered modules. `define-module` emits a module once
  and ensures its required modules are included first. A custom component
  can use the same modules, definitions, getters, and resolver system as
  built-in components.

## Page structure

1. Read all supplied files completely and identify their public APIs,
   source order, doc comments, tags, and relevant implementation details.
2. Choose a clear page title and a concise `description` in the
   frontmatter. Use `outline: deep` for a long reference page when
   appropriate.
3. Begin with a short introduction that starts with "Termeh" and explains
   the page's user-facing purpose.
4. Organize APIs under clear `##` headings in source order. Skip private
   APIs whose names start with `-`. Group closely related APIs where it
   improves navigation, without omitting any public API.
5. Add an appendix only for advanced or raw-value APIs that are clearly
   secondary to the main API.
6. Save the page as `<page-name>.md` in the documentation folder named by
   the user. For one source file, use its name without the leading `_`
   and `.scss`. For multiple files, use a name the user supplied or a
   short kebab-case name for the shared topic. If no folder is given,
   show the Markdown in chat.
7. Check the finished page against the final checklist.

## Frontmatter and introduction

Every page starts with YAML frontmatter containing a generated
`description:`. This description is a short, headline-style summary used
by AI docs to understand and surface the page. Write one sentence that
says what the page covers and what it helps developers do; do not merely
repeat the page title. For example: "Define and use spacing gaps in a
Termeh project." Keep any other frontmatter fields the user explicitly
requests.

The introduction is one to three short sentences. Start with "Termeh"
as the subject, for example "Termeh provides..." or "Termeh includes...".
Explain the overall capability and when a developer would use it; do not
list every API.

## API sections

- Use one `##` section per public API, or group closely related APIs
  under an informative heading and use `###` headings for each API.
- Use a readable Title Case heading (`define-gap` becomes `Define Gap`).
- Explain what the API does and when to use it in one or two short
  sentences. Do not repeat parameter details. For functions, state what
  value they return.
- Put an API signature in a `scss` code block using the actual
  parameter names and defaults, but never include type annotations.
  Follow the reference style, for example:

  ```scss
  @mixin define-gap($name, $value) {}

  @function size($name) {}
  ```

- Put parameter details in a table immediately after the signature.
  Include a table only when the API has parameters. Use this exact shape
  and compact separator:

  ```markdown
  | Parameter | Type | Description |
  | -- | -- | -- |
  ```

- Keep parameter descriptions short, with no trailing period. Describe
  the value rather than repeating the parameter name. Mention a default
  only when useful, using inline code for literal values.
- Type information belongs in the table's `Type` column, not in
  signatures or examples. Write every type name in lowercase and wrap it
  in a single `*` pair, for example `*string*`, `*list\<string\>*`, or
  `*\**`. For multiple accepted types, wrap each type separately and
  separate them with commas, for example `*string*, *null*`.
- Keep generic angle brackets escaped in table text, such as
  `*map\<string, color\>*`. Use `*\**` for any Sass value and
  `*arglist\<string\>*` for variadic string parameters.
- An API with parameters can use a `::: signature` container to group
  its signature, parameter table, and one example. Close the container
  with `:::`. For parameterless APIs, use a simple signature block or
  the container when it helps keep a content-block example with the API.

## Examples

- Include at most one useful example per API. Omit it if a correct,
  practical example cannot be written confidently.
- Use `termeh.` in examples and realistic names and values.
- Keep code blocks free of parameter or return type annotations. Do not
  add types to usage examples.
- Keep examples short and formatted consistently. Use one declaration
  per line, two-space indentation, and expanded content blocks when
  they improve readability.
- Add language identifiers to fenced code blocks when known, such as
  `scss` or `bash`. Optional VitePress code-group labels may be used for
  genuinely equivalent commands.

## Errors, warnings, and supporting notes

- Use a `::: error` block only when the API can throw. State the
  conditions established by `@throw`, `@error`, assertions, or the
  implementation in one concise sentence beginning with "Throw error
  if". Wrap a type named in an error sentence in `*`, such as
  `*string*`. Do not repeat unrelated implementation details.
- Use VitePress containers such as `::: info`, `::: tip`, `::: warn`,
  and `::: alert` for useful supporting information. Keep warnings
  limited to real constraints; do not add decorative callouts.
- Use tables for available values, dependencies, and API relationships
  when they make the information easier to scan. Keep them compact:

  ```markdown
  | Name | Description |
  | -- | -- |
  ```

- Escape literal `|` inside table cells as `\|`. Escape `<` and `>` in
  table text outside inline code.
- Use `@param` for parameter descriptions, `@output` and `@content` for
  API behavior and examples, `@throw` for errors, and `@require` for
  documented module or palette dependencies. The implementation confirms
  these comments; it does not justify adding undocumented behavior.

## Dependency tables

Group documented dependencies by the function used in `@require`. Give
each function its own table, preceded by a short sentence identifying
the API or component and the function, as in "This mixin uses the
following Termeh global `var()`:" or "Button module uses the following
Termeh `variant()`:".

Use these exact columns, in order:

| Function | Table columns |
| -- | -- |
| `var()` | Component, Property, Usage |
| `color()` | Palette, Variant, Usage |
| `variant()` | Palette, Variant, Usage |
| `variant-for()` | Component, Palette, Variant, Usage |

Use the documented arguments for each row and describe its purpose in
Usage. For `color()`, use `-` in Variant because it reads the palette's
base color, not a named variant. Keep parameterized names as documented;
do not invent a fixed palette or variant. List module dependencies
separately from these function-specific tables.

For regular API sections, place dependency descriptions and tables in
blockquotes inside the `::: signature` container, after the example, as
in the mixin reference. For component pages, put them in the relevant
`::: block dependencies` container, as in the button page. Use separate
tables and introductory sentences even when several functions appear in
the same container.

## Component pages

For component style mixins, usually named `use-*`, follow this order.
Keep the section names and detail grounded in the doc comments and source;
omit optional sections when the component has no such feature.

1. **Overview:** Explain what the module renders and its main purpose.
2. **Signature and example:** Show the untyped mixin signature, a
   parameter table with lowercase types, and a valid `termeh.` usage
   example.
3. **Module tip:** Add a `::: tip` stating the exact name under which the
   module is registered in the module system.
4. **Demo:** When the component has a demo, put it in a
   `::: block Demo` container. Include the VitePress preview and a
   fenced HTML source example for that preview inside the same block.
   Prefer a demo that shows all supported modifiers and variations.
5. **Element modifiers:** Use a `## Modifiers` section with a bulleted
   list. Explain each static modifier supported by the main element,
   one modifier per bullet.
6. **Generated modifiers:** Document each input that generates
   modifiers, such as `$sizes` and `$colors`, in its own section. Explain
   the input, the resulting class pattern, and where the available
   values come from. When generated color modifiers depend on palette
   variants, include a `::: block dependencies` container in that
   section, with function-specific tables listing the required variants
   and their uses.
7. **Container:** If present, explain the container and list its
   supported modifiers in bullets.
8. **Children:** If present, explain each child element and list its
   supported modifiers in bullets. For example, document a grid's
   `column` child separately from the grid container.
9. **Customization:** End with this section when the component has
   `@require` tags. In `::: block dependencies`, list every documented
   requirement and its purpose, grouped into separate module and
   function-specific dependency tables as applicable. Do not omit
   requirements or infer dependencies not documented in `@require`
   comments. Keep this section last.

For modules that are not component styles, use the regular API format.
Explain registration or dependencies only when they affect how a
developer uses the API.

## Formatting markers

Only use the following inline emphasis forms. Do not use `=`, `_`, `~`,
`@`, Markdown `**bold**`, or other custom inline markers to style text.

| Form | Meaning | Example |
| -- | -- | -- |
| `__text__` | Bold | `__scheme__` |
| `*text*` | Italic | `*fallback*` |
| `*__text__*` | Blue bold italic | `*__CSS variables__*` |
| `__*text*__` | Red bold italic for critical information | `__*only once*__` |

Use these forms sparingly and consistently. Do not use red emphasis for
ordinary terms or routine warnings. VitePress syntax such as admonitions,
fenced-code language labels, and inline code remains valid; these are
structural/code formatting, not emphasis markers.

## Writing style

- Write clear, natural English for developers using Termeh.
- Be concise and direct. Include only details that help developers
  choose, configure, or use the API.
- Prefer short sentences and familiar words. Avoid filler, marketing
  language, and unnecessary implementation details.
- Do not repeat the same information in the introduction, explanation,
  table, and example.
- End prose sentences with a period. Keep table descriptions as short
  phrases without a trailing period.

## Final checklist

1. The page has frontmatter with a generated, concise, AI-facing
   `description` headline.
2. It starts with a short introduction that begins with "Termeh".
3. The doc comments are the primary source and implementation details
   have been checked.
4. Public APIs are documented in source order; private APIs are skipped.
5. Signatures and examples contain no type annotations.
6. Parameter types appear only in the table's `Type` column, are
   lowercase, and each is wrapped in a single `*` pair.
7. Errors are documented only when supported by the source and use one
   concise "Throw error if" sentence.
8. Only the four documented emphasis forms are used; no `=`, `_`, `~`,
   `@`, or Markdown `**` emphasis remains.
9. Tables use compact `| -- |` separators and escape literal pipes.
10. The page is concise, accurate, and saved in the requested location,
    or shown in chat when no folder was supplied.
11. Component pages follow the required order, include all documented
    modifiers and `@require` dependencies, and end with Customization.
12. Dependency tables are separate for each function, use the prescribed
    columns, and each has its own introductory sentence.
